issues.legal_issue: A registered lease containing conditional successive extensions may state a total duration of at least twelve years, excluding the lessee from thika-tenant status.
material_facts: The registered lease initially specified ten years and provided for two successive five-year extensions if the lessee met stated conditions, followed by an option for a further extension of up to one year.
The lease used the term “extension,” and its schedule described the lease as being for a stipulated period of twenty years.
The dispute concerned whether the lessees acquired thika-tenant status under the applicable tenancy law.
issues.conclusion: The lease was for a stated duration of at least twelve years, so the lessees did not acquire thika-tenant status under the statutory definition.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(5)(b) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, a person holding land under a registered lease whose duration is expressly stated to be at least twelve years is excluded from the definition of a thika tenant. A contract must be construed by reference to its object and all its terms, read as a whole, and its meaning may be gathered from the surrounding provisions and circumstances. An extension ordinarily prolongs the same lease, unlike a renewal, which requires a new lease. The Court applied N.E. Railway v. Hastings, [1900] A.C. 260, on construing an instrument as a whole. It distinguished Kanai Lal v. Paramnidhi, Mahadeolal Kanodia v. Administrator General of West Bengal, Annapuma v. Tincowrie Dutt, Shaffiuddin v. G.C. Banerjee, and Sheikh Gufan v. S.K. Ganguli as not determining the issue on these facts.

rule.if: thika_status_dispute and registered_lease and lease_terms_provide_successive_extensions and lease_schedule_states_term_of_at_least_twelve_years

predicates.thika_status_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a person holding land has thika-tenant status.
predicates.registered_lease: The land is held under a registered lease.
predicates.lease_terms_provide_successive_extension: The lease provides that the same lease may continue for successive additional periods if stated conditions are met.
predicates.lease_schedule_states_term_of_at_least_t: The lease schedule states an overall stipulated term of at least twelve years.
predicates.lessee_is_not_thika_tenant: The lessee does not qualify as a thika tenant under the statutory definition.

issues.definition: When a thika-status dispute concerns a registered lease that provides for successive extensions and states an overall term of at least twelve years, the lessee is not a thika tenant.

issues.legal_issue: Prior proceedings and conduct do not bar a landlord from disputing a tenant’s claimed statutory status when no prior adjudication established that status and the requirements for waiver or estoppel are absent.
material_facts: Earlier proceedings before a tenancy controller did not produce an order finally determining that the lessees had thika-tenant status; one proceeding ended in a compromise.
The Supreme Court had dismissed an earlier petition without deciding whether the tenancy statute applied.
The landlord brought the ejectment suit after acquiring the land, and no covenant to treat the lessees as thika tenants was shown to run with the land.
The evidence did not establish a voluntary, intentional relinquishment of a known right or conduct causing the detriment required for estoppel.
issues.conclusion: The earlier proceedings did not establish the lessees’ statutory status or create res judicata, waiver, or estoppel barring the landlord’s claim.
issues.legal_principle: Waiver requires a voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a known right, or conduct warranting that inference, at an opportunity to choose whether to assert the right. Estoppel does not require an intent to surrender a right, but requires detriment to the other party from the conduct relied on. The Court considered estoppel in the context of section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. A prior proceeding that did not determine the claimed status cannot establish that status as res judicata. Under Shanti Devi v. A.K. Banerjee, [1981] 2 SCC 199, pleadings cannot alter the intrinsic character of a lease or change the rights and obligations flowing from its terms.

rule.if: tenancy_status_dispute and prior_proceedings_concerned_tenant_status and no_final_order_determined_status and no_intentional_relinquishment_of_right and no_detrimental_reliance

predicates.tenancy_status_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a person has statutory tenant status.
predicates.prior_proceedings_concerned_tenant_statu: Earlier proceedings involved the same claimed tenant status.
predicates.no_final_order_determined_status: The earlier proceedings produced no final order determining the claimed status.
predicates.no_intentional_relinquishment_of_right: The person asserting the right did not voluntarily and intentionally relinquish it when there was an opportunity to choose whether to assert it.
predicates.no_detrimental_reliance: The other party did not suffer detriment in reliance on the conduct said to create an estoppel.
predicates.prior_proceedings_do_not_bar_landlord_cl: The earlier proceedings and conduct do not bar the landlord from pursuing the claim.

issues.definition: When a tenant-status dispute follows earlier proceedings that did not finally determine the status, and there was neither intentional relinquishment nor detrimental reliance, those proceedings and conduct do not bar the landlord’s claim.
